reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Bailey & Love (paediatric surgery)
clinicalPearls: Arises from incomplete rotation and fixation of the midgut, leaving a narrow mesenteric base that predisposes to twisting (volvulus)
The classic presentation is a previously well neonate who develops sudden bilious vomiting, which must be treated as a surgical emergency until proven otherwise
Bilious vomiting in an infant should trigger urgent imaging because midgut volvulus can infarct the entire small bowel within hours
The upper gastrointestinal contrast study is the key investigation, showing an abnormally positioned duodenojejunal junction and a corkscrew or spiral appearance if volvulus is present
Ultrasound may reveal an inverted relationship of the superior mesenteric artery and vein or a whirlpool sign of twisted mesentery
Abnormal peritoneal (Ladd) bands can cross and obstruct the duodenum even without volvulus, producing intermittent obstructive symptoms

The definitive operation is the Ladd procedure: untwisting the volvulus, dividing Ladd bands, broadening the mesenteric base, and placing the bowel in a non-rotated position, usually with appendicectomy
Some children present later in life with intermittent, vague abdominal pain or feeding difficulty rather than acute obstruction
reference.pathophysiology: During normal development the midgut herniates, rotates counterclockwise around the superior mesenteric artery, and returns to the abdomen with broad mesenteric fixation. In malrotation this process is incomplete, so the caecum sits abnormally and the mesenteric root is short and narrow. This narrow pedicle allows the midgut to twist around the superior mesenteric vessels, compromising blood supply and causing ischaemia, while abnormal fibrous bands may simultaneously compress the duodenum and produce obstruction.
additionalInvestigations: Upper gastrointestinal contrast series to locate the duodenojejunal junction
Abdominal ultrasound to assess superior mesenteric vessel orientation and look for a whirlpool sign
Plain abdominal radiograph, which may show a paucity of distal gas or a double-bubble pattern
Blood gas and lactate to detect metabolic acidosis suggesting bowel ischaemia
Baseline bloods and cross-match in preparation for emergency laparotomy
redFlags: Bilious vomiting in a neonate or infant, which mandates emergency evaluation for midgut volvulus
Abdominal distension, tenderness, or rectal bleeding suggesting established bowel ischaemia
Rapidly worsening metabolic acidosis or haemodynamic instability indicating strangulated midgut requiring immediate laparotomy
Any delay in diagnosis, as the whole midgut can become necrotic within a few hours of volvulus
reference.prognosis: When volvulus is corrected before ischaemia sets in, outcomes are excellent with low recurrence after a Ladd procedure. Delayed presentation with extensive bowel infarction can necessitate massive resection, leading to short bowel syndrome and long-term nutritional dependence, and carries significant mortality.
pitfalls: Dismissing bilious vomiting as feed intolerance or reflux and delaying imaging
Assuming a normal plain radiograph excludes malrotation or volvulus
Failing to arrange emergency surgery once volvulus is suspected while awaiting further tests
Overlooking older children with intermittent symptoms in whom malrotation is still possible
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
